item.title: What Happens When Your Name Becomes an Insult?
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

What Happens When Your Name Becomes an Insult?

"Karen" memes targeted entitled behavior, but created enduring stigma.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • A new study shows how women named Karen have become judged more negatively.
  • Karens report being insulted and reluctant to disclose their first name.
  • A label condemning bad behavior has created unintended stigma.

What’s in a name? A lot. They are core to who we are. They connect us to our family histories, and can suggest a person’s gender, religion, age, or ethnic identity. We answer to them but are also judged by them.

Popularity of names grows and wanes based on their wider associations. Adolf is not encountered too often these days, whereas Ariel has been on an impressive rise. The changing meanings names communicate is also illustrative of how shifting cultural judgments can manifest in seemingly unexpected ways as a new stigma-by-association. Just ask any Karen.

A new study just out in the journal Self and Identity shows how how changing associations has painfully shifted a common English-language name considered ordinary to a widely recognized insult and a stereotype that then morphed into a stigma.

“Karen” emerged as shorthand for a typically White and behaviorally combative woman perceived as using entitlement or prejudice to police others, particularly service workers and people with less social power. Exactly why “Karen” became the tag for the stereotype of annoying White middle-aged women is vague. But it seems to have solidified in 2020. This was when a viral video of “central park Karen” attracted large-scale public attention, involving a woman whose name was in fact Amy. Other incidents following in which White women were captured calling or threatening to call the police on Black individuals were more specifically and variously identified as “BBQ Becky,” “Permit Patty,” and “Bus Berater Brenda,” among others, but none of them were actually called Karen. Yet by the summer of 2020, “Karen” had gone viral with its newly acquired second meaning.

The new study seeks to understand what being a post-2020 “Karen” now means to those both having and hearing the name. In their first round of data collection, the psychologists asked U.S. college students to provide their reaction to “a Karen,” “a Kathy,” someone named Karen, and someone named Kathy. Kathy was chosen as a comparison because the two names sound somewhat similar and followed comparable historical patterns of popularity.

Unsurprisingly, participants viewed the stereotypical “Karen” as much colder and indicated that they would be much more willing to ignore or exclude her than a stereotypical “Kathy.” More importantly, the judgment spilled over from being “a Karen” to being named Karen. Participants rated a person named Karen as colder—and said they would be more willing to ignore or reject her—than someone named Kathy. The differences were considerably smaller than those involving the full stereotype.

The sample of student reactions also suggested a surprising comfort with the insult. Most considered it at least moderately acceptable to call someone “a Karen” based on bossy or entitled behavior, and the same percentage thought “Karen” jokes acceptable. The surveyed students clearly understood that a person named Karen was not necessarily “a Karen.” But the name alone still seemingly shifted their impressions of people named Karen in a negative direction.

The authors' second study explored the implications of such view on 195 women named Karen, located through a Facebook group of people sharing the name. While this is not a presentative sample, results do suggest that those with the name reported significant and sometimes highly distressing treatment based on their name. More than three-quarters agreed that people had insulted them because of their name and two-thirds reported hesitation in sharing their name. Smaller proportions reported apparent name-based discrimination by employers, educators, or health professionals. As one participant named Karen said: “Now if I hear someone call me by my name, I cringe.”

Interestingly and importantly, the insult also has a gendered quality. The study authors note that that there is no comparably established male equivalent. “Karen” may thus sometimes penalize women for expressions of anger or assertiveness that would attract less comment from men. Thus the term can function both as a critique of White privilege while also reproducing misogynistic ideas about how women should behave.

Psychologists call such phenomena stigma by association or courtesy stigma. Usually, it describes the devaluation experienced by someone closely connected to a stigmatized person, such as a family member or friend. Here, the association is unusually thin. There need be no relationship. A first name is enough to connote someone who is rude, annoying, loud and entitled.

This demonstrates how easily and quickly and new stigmas can emerge, gain momentum, and travel far despite having no meaningful or tangible connection to the people who then become targeted. In this case, repeated jokes, memes, and casual insults carried in social media rapidly changed the cultural meaning of the name itself. Women named Karen—including the many who are delightful people—are then left to manage the consequences. They now discover a world in which they must tolerate jokes, explain themselves, adopt nicknames, and pause before introducing themselves.

This exposes one of social stigma’s underlying mechanisms. We can consciously reject the idea that a stereotype applies to a particular person, yet the association can still quietly shape how we feel about and behave toward them. Not surprisingly, Karen has dropped markedly in popularity among baby names. Stigmas of course over time can diminish. But in my several decades of studying stigma I have observed that this rarely happens as quickly or as readily. Stigmas tend to stick once they have entered the cultural zeitgeist, with ongoing collateral damage. Karens are bearing the cost.

item.title: Why We're in a New Golden Age of Horror Movies
item.description:
Fear

Why We're in a New Golden Age of Horror Movies

Scary movies may be a symptom of anxious times —and a way to cope with them.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Horror movies are drawing huge audiences and winning Oscars, a rare event for the genre.
  • The appetite for horror may grow with collective anxiety, as Stephen King suggested in 1981.
  • Scary fiction may work as threat simulation: a safe way to rehearse fear and build coping capacity.

“What’s your favorite scary movie?”

That question became famous because of 1996’s hit horror movie Scream. It was posed to Drew Barrymore’s ill-fated character, who hesitated before answering, and the question has only become harder since. Today, in 2026, there is just so much good stuff to choose from. We are living in a new Golden Age of horror. Hundreds of new horror movies come out each year, and while far from all of them are worth your time, the top-shelf stuff alone is incredibly abundant.

Just within the last couple of years, we have seen a crop of well-made and genuinely frightening horror movies draw huge audiences, such as Sinners (2025), Weapons (2025), Backrooms (2026), and Obsession (2026). Obsession, made for a measly million dollars at most, garnered more than $500 million in revenue. Both Sinners and Weapons won Oscars, a pretty rare event for a horror movie, and Sinners did so after a record 16 nominations. And Backrooms as well as Obsession were, surprisingly, directed by industry outsiders who had cut their cinematic teeth creating YouTube content.

Horror films’ share of North American box office revenue, 1995–2025. In 2025 the genre took 16.2 percent, up from 4.4 percent a decade earlier.
Source: Graphic: Mathias Clasen, made with Claude (Anthropic). Data: The Numbers.

Why Horror Is Booming

There are many reasons for the current boom. With streaming, even the weirdest horror movie finds its audience. Horror is cheap to make and needs neither stars nor a familiar franchise, so a hit pays back many times over. It is also one of the few genres that still gets young people into theaters at a time when superhero sequels are faltering. And after centuries of suspicion—frightening entertainment has been accused of being morally corrosive, psychologically harmful, and symptomatic of a sick society, none of which is true—horror is finally climbing the cultural hierarchy.

Scary Times, Scary Movies

The one factor I want to zoom in on, however, is psychological, and perhaps a little paradoxical. I think a major reason for the current abundance (and box office success) of horror is that the appetite for horror increases with society-level anxiety.

Many people feel that we are living in unprecedentedly frightening times; that the world is scarier than it used to be, with war, political unrest and extreme polarization, shifting geopolitical tectonics, climate change fostering a helpless sort of dread, and so on. It makes intuitive sense that a frightening world would produce frightening fiction. But why would people want more of it?

We have discussed this in the Recreational Fear Lab, because that’s the sort of thing we discuss when we meet for lunch. Our ambition, after all, is to chart the psychological engine room of people’s tendency to wring pleasure from frightening activities. One compelling hypothesis comes from the master of horror, Stephen King, who in his 1981 nonfiction book about horror, Danse Macabre, suggested that “we make up horrors to help us cope with the real ones.” He went on to explain that the horror genre seems to achieve extraordinary popularity at certain historical moments that “almost always seem to coincide with periods of fairly serious economic and/or political strain.” The horror books and films that become popular during such times, said King, “seem to reflect those free-floating anxieties (for want of a better term) which accompany such serious but not mortal dislocations.”

Evidence From the Pandemic

Could King be right? There is some indirect evidence.

First, consider Contagion, a 2011 movie about a deadly new virus. It did respectable business when it came out, then shot up the rental and streaming charts in the early days of the COVID pandemic. The scenario depicted in the film suddenly seemed terribly relevant, and people were looking for ways to understand their unsettling reality. Fiction provided a map for the uncharted territory in which they found themselves.

Second, consider a study conducted in our lab (Scrivner et al., 2021) during the darkest days of pandemic lockdown, in the spring of 2020. Societies were closing down, the streets were as empty as the supermarket shelves, the news showed footage of overflowing morgues—it all seemed like something out of a zombie movie, sans zombies.

We set out to investigate whether horror fans were more psychologically resilient during those frightening times, on the premise that when you watch a horror movie, you practice emotion regulation. You suppress fear and anxiety in order to not be overwhelmed, and to hit that sweet spot of fear (Andersen et al., 2020). And horror fans did turn out to be more resilient. Moreover, fans of prepper movies—movies about the end of the world, zombie apocalypses, alien invasions, and so on—felt better prepared for whatever the immediate future might throw at them. That’s why we called the article “Pandemic Practice.” We also found that morbidly curious people were more interested in pandemic movies during the pandemic: Their appetite rose with the threat. The study was correlational, so it may simply be that resilient people are drawn to horror. But the pattern fits King’s idea.

Horror stories may help us imaginatively prep. They allow us to rehearse, in the safety of our imaginations, worst-case scenarios, and in the process build coping capacity. In a sense, it’s not that different from soldiers spending thousands of hours simulating combat so that they are ready for the real thing. Horror, likewise, can function as a form of threat simulation (Clasen et al., 2020).

Symptom and Cure

The current boom in horror movies may thus tell us something about our culture—it may be a symptom of a frightened society. But curiously, it may also be the cure. By imaginatively exposing ourselves to fictional depictions of our darkest fears—the fear that we are failing to protect our children in Weapons, say, or the fear of what loneliness and romantic entitlement can turn into in Obsession, or the unease of a life lived online in Backrooms—we improve our coping capacity. Those movies convert our “free-floating anxieties” into tangible fear, which can be resolved. This idea is speculative for now, but it is a thesis that we are hoping to investigate scientifically in the Lab.

So the next time someone asks about your favorite scary movie, take your time. There has never been more to choose from, and watching may do you some good.

item.title: When "Let's Agree to Disagree" Becomes a Cemetery
item.description:
Relationships

When "Let's Agree to Disagree" Becomes a Cemetery

Some arguments end. Others just get buried and may come back as ghosts

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • "Let's agree to disagree" brings relief, but said too often it becomes a cemetery for unresolved issues.
  • At work, a boss can settle what stays unsettled. In a relationship, there is no boss.
  • Fidelity and trust are the terms a relationship runs on. We cannot agree to disagree about them.
  • Ask yourself: if this stays unresolved for a year, what will decide it?

She remembers very well when he said it for the first time in their relationship: "Let's agree to disagree." She felt immediately relieved. The argument was going nowhere anyway. It was about what they should get for a friend's wedding. Nothing that would shake their relationship. Two years, many arguments and many "let's agree to disagree" later, nothing is left to discuss, not even important questions such as when cheating starts or whether they should get pregnant. The phrase "let's agree to disagree" has turned into a cemetery where many unresolved issues lie buried.

Let's move to an office. Someone says, "Let's agree to disagree," laptops close, and the whiteboard still holds two options with a question mark between them. No one knows what the outcome is, and, much worse, no one knows what to do next. But at the workplace there is always a boss, a manager, who can turn "agree to disagree" into "what we must agree on." In a relationship, there is no boss.

Two Ways to Agree to Disagree

In the first, the phrase works like a bookmark. The disagreement is acknowledged, left on the record, and either person can return to it. In the second, it works like a closed file. The topic is declared finished, and whatever each person still believes goes underground.

Call it the polite verdict: "agree to disagree" spoken by someone who has privately concluded that the other person is wrong. The words announce a truce; the conclusion underneath does not move.

There is one subject on which agreeing to disagree does not work: the terms a relationship runs on. What counts as fidelity, what trust requires, what each person may keep private—these are not opinions held side by side. They are an agreement in force every day, spoken or not.

Agreeing to disagree on such a term does not set it aside. It leaves two private rulebooks running at once. When they collide, one partner may experience as betrayal what the other experienced as nothing at all.

When a Phrase Helps, and When It Harms

It tends to help when the disagreement concerns taste or personal interests rather than shared facts or shared terms, when no joint decision depends on it, when either person could raise it again without penalty, and when both are genuinely willing to call the other's view different rather than mistaken.

It tends to harm when a shared decision is still pending, when one person is privately delivering a polite verdict, when the person with more power uses it to close the subject, and when the same topic keeps returning and feels less resolvable each time. On the terms of the relationship itself, it does not belong at all.

One question sorts most cases: If this stays unresolved for a year, what will decide it? If the answer is that nothing needs deciding, the truce is probably sound. If the answer is the status quo, or whoever holds the most power, the conversation has not ended. It has been handed off.

If disagreement in a relationship comes with fear, or one person cannot safely voice a different view, that is not a difference of opinion. A licensed therapist or a confidential support service can help sort out what is happening.

Keeping Disagreement Visible

None of this means every disagreement must be argued to a conclusion. Some differences are permanent and harmless, and treating them as problems to solve can do its own damage. The permission needed is not to fight on but to keep the disagreement visible: named, remembered, and open to return, even when no one is ready to resolve it.

item.title: What Keeps Women Growing as They Get Older?
item.description:
Aging

What Keeps Women Growing as They Get Older?

Curiosity can help us adapt to changes and remain more engaged throughout life.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Curiosity can help older adults remain engaged, adaptable, and open to learning.
  • Aging well includes learning to hold loss and appreciation at the same time.
  • Growing older can bring greater clarity about where to place one's time and attention.
Source: Yuri Arcurs / Envato, Licensed image used with permission.

I cannot say exactly when I became “old." I look in the mirror and see “an old lady with a young woman inside” (my mother’s words upon seeing her own reflection). She lived robustly until her death, just days before her 98th birthday. Most of my other relatives died well before the age I am now.

As with many women, I feel lucky to be alive. Like them, I recognize that simply arriving at this point is evidence of luck and inner resources. Along the way, we succeeded, stumbled, adapted, and began again with resilience. Now, I am curious to discover what lies ahead.

I am particularly interested in how women create meaningful, engaged lives as they age: lives rich with purpose, confidence, creativity, connection, and joy.

At 40, I began giving seminars about “aging well” to people ranging from their 60s to their 90s. I watched and listened carefully to my students’ observations about growing old.

This is what I learned.

Developing Wisdom and Self-Trust

Aging well requires weaving difficulty into our lives without allowing it to become our whole story. The wisdom we acquire through relationships, work, illness, caregiving, love, disappointment, and loss can help us meet an uncertain present with a more realistic view of ourselves and life.

As many women grow older, they become more attentive to their needs and values. Recovering from mistakes, losses, and challenges they once believed were unthinkable contributes to feeling steadier and grateful. They learn to trust their judgment, feel less compelled to please others at the expense of their own well-being, and care less that some consider them invisible.

Spending Time Wisely

Recognizing how precious time is, women pay close attention to how they spend it. A heightened curiosity compels them to explore what interests and resonates with them. They may become more confident, willing to try something new, and say what they think. They choose people and experiences that offer peace, wonder, adventure, and renewal. They become intentional and mindful about where they focus their attention.

An enormous industry, as well as a growing body of science, is devoted to longevity and “turning back the hands of time.” I am less interested in turning back time than in understanding how we can live well within the time, however brief, that is ours.

I am fascinated by how our attitudes and beliefs influence our experience of aging—and how illness, loss, relationships, purpose, and our daily choices affect the way we see ourselves as participants in our lives.

Staying Curious

Research and my own clinical work repeatedly point to one quality of aging well: curiosity. “People tend to quickly forget information that doesn’t engage their curiosity,” remarks Alan D. Castel, PhD, who continues, “... as we get older, we don’t want to stop learning. We’re just more selective about what we want to learn … a lot of older adults will go back to take classes or pick up hobbies or engage in bird watching … this level of curiosity, if maintained, can really keep us sharp as we age.”

Curiosity helps us remain open when life changes. Instead of asking only, “Why is this happening to me?” we might also ask, “What do I need now? What can I learn? How can I adapt?” This type of inquiry contributes to our resilience.

In one five-year study of older adults, greater curiosity was associated with survival. While we do not know definitively whether curiosity itself helps people live longer, staying interested and engaged as we age might allow older adults to cope with the physical and environmental challenges in old age.

Cultivating Resilience

Aging well requires patience, flexibility, adaptation, and the ability to tolerate uncertainty. The phone rings with news that a friend had a stroke, a cousin died, a grandchild is in trouble, an adult child was diagnosed with a serious illness. These realities become part of our personal tapestry.

Along with curiosity, gratitude, patience, adaptability, living with uncertainty, and a sense of wonder help us as we age. They do not erase pain, but they allow pain and appreciation to coexist. We can grieve what has changed while remaining open to what is still here. We can acknowledge loss while noticing beauty. We can feel sorrow and still experience moments of joy. Aging well is living with and allowing conflicting emotions to be part of our experience at the same time.

Selecting Activities With Intention

As younger women, many of us took pride in how many balls we juggled at once. We were praised for (and often inwardly cheered) the amount and variety of balls we kept in the air at once. But when we dropped one or two, we often focused on those rather than appreciating all the ones we kept aloft.

As we get older, we can choose fewer balls, selecting with intention. We might even experiment with holding just one at a time: Visit a sick friend without checking our phone; attend a grandchild’s game and simply watch and cheer; walk outdoors and notice how the light dances through the trees; have a conversation without preparing our response before the speaker is finished.

Continuing to Expand

We can expand our minds while also giving ourselves space. We can continue to discover ourselves throughout life, becoming more fully ourselves. Perhaps one gift of growing older is the freedom to choose more wisely how we occupy our time and where we place our attention. We cannot control everything that accompanies aging, but we can remain curious about who we are becoming and chart our course using that curiosity as our North Star.

item.title: What We Don't Mention on Facebook
item.description:
Social Media

What We Don't Mention on Facebook

Unshared mistakes and rejections that shape our personal narratives.

Posted October 8, 2026

Oops: Bad idea.
Source: Eliezer Sobel/ChatGpt

Most of us, much of the time, are preoccupied with how we are perceived by the world and thus quite concerned with how we present ourselves. The most glaring examples often pointed to are the magical and happy lives depicted on the average Facebook or Instagram feed. However, I’d like to reveal some of the moments I’ve omitted from my social media accounts: the little failures, mishaps, bad luck and rejections that live quietly in the shadows of my personal story:

I was fired from my first job, as a pizza delivery guy, while still in high school. My boss felt that getting hopelessly lost in Hackensack, New Jersey, taking close to two hours to locate a customer who lived ten minutes away, then handing them a cold pizza, did not indicate a real aptitude for the job. There was no GPS in 1970, only torn, barely legible paper maps with microscopic street names I’d study by flashlight on the side of the road.

In college, I only lasted one day working for Time-Life books, making cold calls to convince harried housewives that they desperately needed to purchase a set of books they didn’t want or need, for an exorbitant fee. Each of the salespeople in the room were set up with a desk, a phone, and a large cardboard display containing the precisely scripted words we were to use on the calls. A supervisor up front was able to listen in on every conversation.

I reached the end of my rope when one woman said, “I’m sorry, but my husband just died, and I can’t talk about this right now.” Rather than simply offering my condolences and hanging up—you know, like a human being might do—I had been trained to scan the script and locate the “Death and Bereavement” section, which instructed me to recite, “Yes, in times of sorrow and loss, there is often nothing more comforting than to curl up with a good book.” When I informed our leader at the end of the day that I wouldn’t be returning, he responded with this hopeful feedback:
“You will never succeed at anything in this life.”

"What's on it?"
Source: Eliezer Sobel/FreeMaker

Ha! Little did he know that I would soon land a spot at Colonel Mustard’s Last Stand, serving hot dogs, and succeeding beyond my wildest dreams! The entire training consisted of memorizing three words: “What’s on it?” Which I nailed! Customers could choose ketchup, mustard, relish, pickles ,or onions. I was paid by the hot dog.

One summer, I was hired as a uniformed security guard by a department store. My job was to stand by the door all day, for which I was rigorously trained by shadowing an old-timer who had been doing the job for years. His training included showing me how to lock up the place at the end of the day by, as he put it, “inserting the key into the lock, and turning it.” Apart from that little kernel, the only other wisdom he imparted to me about the job was to tell me that, “You basically just stand there.” And as it turned out, I was pretty damn good at it. I “just stood there” for two months. The skill set for that career was eclipsed only by my time spent on an assembly line for the Arrow Book Club: cardboard boxes filled with books would fly past me on a conveyorbelt at a lightning pace, and my job was to grab a bundle of tissue paper and stuff it into each box. It was never boring. (If you grew up in the '50s and know the reference, it was a bit like Lucy and the chocolates.)

As a high ropes course instructor, I led groups of executives, college fraternities, and inner-city kids through a harrowing field of challenges way up in the ethers. One Sunday afternoon when the site was empty, I decided to “practice falling,” while strapped into a safety harness, in order to physiologically train my body on a non-verbal, cellular level that falling was safe, and thus rid myself of any lingering fear of heights. What I hadn’t taken into account was that while indeed it was safe to fall, and the safety harness would protect me, it nevertheless left me helplessly dangling from a log, 50 feet in the air, puzzled by this unanticipated challenge.

It occurred to me that I could call a fellow instructor and sheepishly confess my predicament and request a rescue mission, or worse, surrender to hanging in space overnight until the following morning when the staff would arrive to discover an unidentified aerial phenomenon suspended above. After an hour of futile and increasingly desparate attempts, I eventually discovered that by swinging myself back and forth with increasing intensity, I could get one foot up onto the log and then somehow drag the rest of my body to follow. I thought it was a funny anecdote to share with my boss; apparently he didn’t find it amusing. I was let go one day later.

I have a dozen more such tales, but to see how happy and well I am really doing otherwise, please consult my Facebook page.

item.title: Do You Ruminate?
item.description:
Anxiety

Do You Ruminate?

How to get free from negative preoccupation.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Unproductive rumination is a predictor of becoming depressed and staying depressed.
  • Productive rumination leads to action today; unproductive rumination leads to self-criticism.
  • You don’t need an answer to move forward. You need to live your life today.
Source: Ivan S / Pexels

We can define rumination as a repeated negative focus on past or current events, where you dwell on something while trying to make sense of it. You may think, “Why did this happen?” or “I can’t believe this happened.” This continual focus on your thoughts is one of the best predictors of becoming depressed and staying depressed, according to Yale psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema.

The consequence of rumination is that you are focusing on negatives, which will make you feel worse. Also, you may never get an answer that is completely satisfactory if you detach yourself from everyday life and don’t focus on positive goals within your control. People ruminate about past decisions, relationships, and disturbing events. They even ruminate about why they ruminate. The good news is that there are new approaches in cognitive behavioral therapy developed by our colleagues in England—Edward Watkins at the University of Exeter and Adrian Wells at the University of Manchester. Watkins developed Rumination-Focused CBT and Wells independently developed Metacognitive Therapy. Research shows that both therapeutic models can help reverse rumination.

Eight Steps to Reversing Rumination

Let me share with you some steps that you can take and that a therapist can help you with to avoid being hijacked by these intrusive thoughts. It requires some work for the patient, but research shows that these two models can reverse rumination and decrease the depression associated with rumination.

  1. Label your intrusive thoughts as rumination. This can be simply saying to yourself, “I am now ruminating.” This allows you to target the repetitive process that is the real problem.
  2. Examine the cost and benefits to you of ruminating. For example, we know the cost can be depression, distraction, passivity, and isolation. Now you may think there are benefits. For example, you may think that there’s some secret you will discover that will help you make things better in the future. Has this worked for you, or has it simply reinforced rumination? Or you may think you have no control over the rumination, so you don’t have a choice. This is key, since we will see that you do have a choice to do something different from rumination.
  3. Ask if this is productive or unproductive rumination. I have found this distinction helpful when addressing regret, worry, and envy. Productive rumination leads to a practical solution or action. For example, if I have a lecture in two weeks, I might ask, “Are my PowerPoint slides ready?” I can then work on them now. It is productive because it leads to action today—a “to-do list today.” Unproductive rumination focuses on self-criticism: “What is wrong with me that I put this off?” The better response to procrastination is action, not rumination. Taking a step forward is progress.
  4. Turn “why” questions into “how” questions. Instead of asking, “Why did this happen to me?” ask, “What can I do today to improve my life?” Rather than dwelling on a past relationship or decision, choose rewarding and meaningful activities: exercise, spend time with family or friends, address a work problem, or contact someone you care about. Shifting your focus from “why” to “how” empowers you to act on what you can control.
  5. Set aside rumination time. Rather than getting hijacked by your thoughts, you can make an appointment with your rumination later in the day. For example, you can set aside 15 minutes at 3 p.m., and if you have rumination thoughts before that, write them down and set them aside until 3 o’clock. Many people think they’re unable to do that, but I found that a lot of people are able to delay rumination to some extent. At 3 p.m., you may realize it’s the same thoughts over and over, so now you can think, “Why repeat them?” In addition, you may ask yourself if it is productive to keep focusing on this. If not, it’s unproductive rumination, and then you can decide what you can do. What actions can you take that are productive, even if these actions are unrelated to the rumination.
  6. Try accepting that you don’t have an answer. Humans are the only animals looking for an answer. You don’t need an answer; you need to live your life today. What if you accepted that you don’t have an answer for things that happened to you or experiences that you did not like? You can replace looking for an answer with having a goal based on the values and positive things that you can pursue today. Rewards can replace the need for answers. Not everything has to make sense.
  7. Don’t expect everything to be fair. One of the things that people ruminate about is that they have been treated unfairly. Certainly, if you can assert yourself and make things better today, that might be a good course of action. But many times these events are in the past, and the people are in the past. We often get caught up in believing in what’s called the just world. This is the belief that bad things happen to bad people and good things happen to good people. So, if something bad happened to me, I must be a bad person. If we can accept that sometimes unfairness happens to all of us and if there’s no way that we can be assertive to right the wrong, we can understand that rumination would be a waste of time. Rumination will not make things fair.
  8. Use imagery to let go of thoughts. Think about rumination as intrusive, unwanted thoughts. Consider using some of the following images to detach from them. Treat the thought like a telemarketing call that you don’t pick up. Think about the thought as a cloud in the sky that is floating away. Or think about the thought as a train in the station, but you’re not getting on that train. This is called detached mindfulness. When you let go of the rumination, you can get back into a life worth living.

item.title: How You and Your Team Build Judgment in the AI Era
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How You and Your Team Build Judgment in the AI Era

Six practices to help organizations build judgment for professional growth.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Judgment combines personal qualities, knowledge, and experience for better decision-making.
  • AI reduces traditional judgment-building tasks, so organizations must teach judgment intentionally.
  • Leaders should "show their work" to help junior staff develop real-world judgment skills.

Think about a time at work when you had to make an important judgment call. Maybe a client sent an email that was clearly wrong, and you had to decide whether to correct them immediately or pause and consider the consequences. Maybe a colleague made a mistake that could affect a project, and you had to decide whether to raise it, how to raise it, and when. Perhaps you were asked to make a recommendation with incomplete information, or you had to decide whether to trust your instincts when the data seemed to point in another direction.

These moments rarely come with clear instructions. They require you to assess the situation, weigh competing considerations, anticipate consequences, draw on experience, and decide. Sometimes you get it right and sometimes you get in wrong; however, the only way you get better is by reflecting on what happened and learning from the outcome.

Today, AI is forcing organizations to think much more deeply about what judgment is and how people develop it. Judgment is a complex topic, and many organizations don’t know where to start. The goal of this post is to start with the basics: What is judgment and how can it be developed?

What is judgment?

I used to think of judgment as a gut instinct or a feeling that developed over time to produce an insight or to recognize a pattern that others overlooked. While that may be part of it, my favorite definition of judgment comes from Sir Andrew Likierman, a professor at London Business School who has studied the skills and behaviors that create the conditions that allow judgment to bloom. He defines judgment as “the ability to combine personal qualities with relevant knowledge and experience to form opinions and make decisions.” Specifically, there are key practices that you can adopt and skills you can cultivate to help inform the judgments you make. I’ve added some TNTs (tiny noticeable things) to help you begin to operationalize these areas.

The six components of good judgment

According to Likierman’s research, there are six elements of good judgment as follows:

Learning: The first component of judgment is learning—accumulating knowledge and understanding patterns. It’s important to consume information accurately, listening to what is said (and unsaid), and pay close attention to facts.

Trusting Relationships: Having a diverse group of people you can reach out to for advice, opinions, and observation builds judgment. Your onboarding and mentoring programs are an important part of judgment formation, as those are ways in which your employees begin to foster the networks they need. Employees on the edge of the network—those with limited connections—are two to three times more likely to quit. Without strong ties, they are often left out of critical conversations, informal support, and growth opportunities, all things that help build judgment.

Experience: Another way people build judgment is by using past context to spot patterns, recognize challenges, and identify potential paths forward. When I practiced law, I knew I had years to build those capacities. Now, AI is shortening the runway considerably. Leaders need to introduce team members to their reasoning, negotiation dynamics, difficult client conversations, discussion about strategic tradeoffs, post-matter reflection, and escalation decisions. Leaders must now “show their work” in these areas far sooner.

Many leaders are experimenting with technology-driven simulations (great when the stakes are high or dangerous—think healthcare and the military) to help build judgment, but there are other ways to help your team gain experience. One way is to encourage reflection. An after-action review is a common method of debriefing that originated in the military but is widely used in the business world today. Here are some questions you (and your team) can consider:

  • What was the intended outcome?
  • What was the actual outcome?
  • Went went well?
  • What would I/we do differently?

Even though you may be new to a role, you’ve undoubtedly had to make judgment calls about other things in your life. I recently had to wrestle with whether to tell a valued client that I had a poor experience with someone internal to their organization. I thought about other difficult conversations I had in the past, and I decided that it did not make sense to bring it up right now. Think about those past experiences to identify what worked and what didn’t.

Other ways to gain experience include secondments, volunteering for committees, asking senior leaders about their work, asking to be part of an important deal, and talking to the business professionals in your workplace to learn more about how the organization thinks about technology, finance, or operations.

Detachment—Know Your Roadblocks: Another aspect of judgment is understanding your own icebergs and thinking traps so you can see situations clearly. Icebergs are your core values and beliefs about the way you think the world should operate, and they can interfere with your ability to see a situation accurately. I also call them your “rules.” Your rules often involve the words “always,” “never,” or “must.” Some examples of icebergs include, “I always need to be in charge,” “I must have all the answers,” and “strong people don’t ask for help.” Icebergs are often too inflexible to allow you to perform or lead in the way you want.

Options: Judgment calls are rarely black and white. If they were, they wouldn’t have landed on your desk. People are often asked to choose between multiple options. It's important to consider whether there are more options than those presented. For example, other options might include doing nothing or delaying a decision until more information is available. In addition, you must factor in the risks associated with novel solutions or radical options, get clear about rules and ethical issues, and surface peoples’ stakes in the outcome. Good leaders will share their thought processes with junior team members.

Delivery: Finally, good judgment requires careful thought about how a decision will be executed, including the real-world risks of implementation. One way to help facilitate delivery is to conduct a premortem. A premortem is a chance for a team or group to discuss ways a course of action might fail so they can uncover and address problems before they happen.

In its simplest terms, building judgment follows this process:

  • You’re given new responsibilities that stretch you,
  • You make an effort,
  • You succeed or fail and get some feedback, and
  • You learn from that experience.

As AI takes over more work, entry-level roles are losing more of the messy, formative tasks that once served as judgment training grounds. In an AI-enabled workplace, judgment must become something organizations deliberately teach, practice, and develop, and the time to start is now.

item.title: 5 Ways to Move Gratitude From Your Head to Your Heart
item.description:
Gratitude

5 Ways to Move Gratitude From Your Head to Your Heart

Moving gratitude from something you think about to something you actually feel.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude can become an emotional experience, not just a list we run through in our heads.
  • Practicing gratitude can help shift us from a sense of scarcity toward sufficiency and abundance.
  • Small, consistent practices help gratitude become part of who we are and how we see the world.

When we're in a good season and life is going well for us, ask most of us what we're grateful for, and the answers could likely come quickly. We might start by naming the things we know we appreciate... I'm grateful for my family, my health, my home, my work. Yet sometimes, we say it, we think it, and we keep it all above the shoulders. My gentle invitation is to go a little deeper to truly feel it. This matters even more when life feels hard or heavy.

Why Gratitude Matters

The research talks about how gratitude changes us psychologically, emotionally, physiologically, and even spiritually. Gratitude can help calm the nervous system and ease stress while shifting our attention away from negative thought patterns and into the present moment. Research even suggests that gratitude may help lessen symptoms of depression, improve sleep quality, and contribute to a greater overall sense of well-being. In my work, I have also seen that when people make space for gratitude, they are more likely to help others and follow through with the wellness behaviours that support them.

Experiencing and expressing gratitude regularly, even in small doses, can promote a lasting, appreciative perspective on life (Bohlmeijer et al., 2021). Through life's storms and challenges, it can help keep us connected to what is still steady and good, and as with most things, practice makes better.

The Scarcity Lens

Gratitude has a lot to do with perspective. It is a choice that helps us focus on the positive aspects of our lives.

When we're caught in a scarcity mindset, it can become the lens through which we see everything. Not enough time. Not enough opportunities. Not enough money. Not enough recognition. If someone believes there aren't enough opportunities, they will move through the world looking for evidence that it's true. The opportunities may be there, but they may not be primed to notice them. Gratitude helps shift our attention toward what is here and what we do have, moving us toward a greater sense of sufficiency, and even abundance. It's what can help us start to see that we do have enough resources to meet the moment, there is spaciousness in my day, and I do have the right people in my corner.

Gratitude doesn't erase hardship or difficult emotions, and it doesn't mean we need to search for a silver lining. What it can do is strengthen the body's capacity to take in and hold onto the good. This matters especially when we're feeling unsteady, exhausted, or dysregulated.

5 Ways to Feel Your Gratitude, Not Just Think It

  1. Drop into your body: Gratitude can be an emotional experience when we let ourselves really settle into it. The next time you name something you’re grateful for, pause. Picture the person, the moment, or the experience and really feel into the feeling associated with what you are expressing thanks for. Recall the unexpected expression of love, the phone call, the favour you didn’t see coming, or the memory that still makes you smile.
  2. Look for what is here, especially where it feels scarce: When you catch yourself thinking “not enough,” take a moment to notice what is here and what you do have in that moment. If you’re feeling like there’s not enough time, perhaps you have a quiet 20 minutes before dinner. Or if you’re feeling like there’s not enough support, maybe there is one person who would answer if you reached out. Practicing gratitude in the opposite direction of where we’re feeling scarcity can be what helps widen the lens.
  3. Savour the micro moments: Let yourself sit with the appreciation of the little things, like being fully present with a hot cup of coffee. I still find it fascinating that we will spend 20 minutes looking for a show to watch, but many of us struggle to find the time to reflect and count our blessings! Try stacking a pause onto something you already do every day, such as making your coffee, brushing your teeth, or waiting for the kettle. That daily habit is a built-in reminder to notice the small things. Over time, it builds trust that moments of goodness and relief will keep showing up, and that we can lean into them.
  4. Try imagining without: Think about something you count on every day, like hot water in the shower, a reliable car, or that video call with your child when they’re away at school. Imagine what it would feel like not to have it, and then come back to the reality that you do. The everyday gifts, conveniences, and connections we sometimes overlook tend to light up when we picture their absence.
  5. Remember what you once wished for: On any given day, I recognize that my life is made up of things I once prayed for. When I am deeply present in this place of gratitude, it can bring me to my knees. How much of your life today is made up of things you once wished for and worked for? Blessings hit harder when you remember what you went through to experience them.

Final Thoughts

Gratitude can set the soul ablaze and bring us into a deeper appreciation for the little things that aren't so little after all.

By intentionally building and fostering gratitude practices, they eventually become part of who we are, how we show up, and how we see the world. Before the day gets busy, even saying, "Thank you for this new day," can change how we meet the day ahead. Perhaps by slowing down enough to really appreciate the moments and gifts, we can remember just how precious this big, beautiful life can be.

item.title: Wild Minds and the Value of Diversifying Brain Research
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Wild Minds and the Value of Diversifying Brain Research

Kelly Lambert's new book stresses the importance of research in the wild.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Read about a mischievous raccoon, a shape-shifting octopus, and elephants who engage in deceptive behavior.
  • Lambert argues the need for advancing mental health through more ecologically informed strategies.
  • She stresses neuroplasticity and is interested in how environments and experiences shape brains.
Source: Willemijn Doelman/Pexels.

As someone who has done extensive work on captive and wild animals, I've always been concerned about how data collected in different research environments—different captivity conditions, different field sites, and active versus fieldwork on members of the same species—compare with one another. Recently, I've been especially interested in how well research on captive, controlled dogs translates to free-ranging and feral dogs.

However, this doesn't mean any particular research project lacks rigor; instead, it's how robust and generalizable the data are. We can be careful when making sweeping generalizations using data collected in different places. These are among the many reasons I was keenly interested in neuroscientist Dr. Kelly Lambert's wide-ranging new book Wild Brains: What Animals Can Teach Us About Being Well, in which she "invites readers on a captivating journey to rethink traditional animal research models, venturing beyond the confines of the laboratory to explore the extraordinary promise of studying animal brains in the wild."

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Wild Brains?

Kelly Lambert: I was trained as a laboratory-focused neuroscientist, and I still value the discoveries that laboratory neuroscience has produced. But as a behavioral neuroscientist, I’ve always been fascinated by the complexity of animals’ lives and the different ways species have evolved to thrive in their habitats.

The final nudge came when a wild rat broke into my histology lab. It knocked over sugar used in one of our protocols and built a nest from a shredded neuroscience journal and pieces of sheep brain left from a student lab practical. We’ve heard of city rats and country rats; I had encountered an academic rat!

The wild rat’s resourcefulness stood in striking contrast to the docile, selectively bred laboratory rats just down the hall. That encounter helped propel my research toward wild rats and other species. I wrote Wild Brains to explore animals in the context of their actual lives, in habitats they evolved to live in. I also hope the book encourages young neuroscientists to broaden the species and environments they study. Nontraditional approaches and models may provide fresh ways to investigate enduring questions about human brain health.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

KL: My graduate training was behavioral neuroscience, with an emphasis on comparative animal behavior. Over nearly four decades of studying brains and behavior, the comparative side of that training took the back seat. Meanwhile, I focused on laboratory rats. I even wrote a book about what they taught me, The Lab Rat Chronicles.

My curiosity about other species, however, never went away. Since early in my career, I’ve conducted observational research with macaques at Monkey Jungle and the DuMond Conservancy near Miami. I’ve also been fascinated by raccoons since childhood, which eventually led me to study their behavior and brains.

The theme that connects Wild Brains with my past lab research is experience-based neuroplasticity, the theme of my laboratory research. Essentially, we’re interested in how environments and experiences shape brains. Wild Brains allowed me to explore that question across a much wider range of animals.

Source: Princeton University Press/with permission.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

KL: Can I say anyone with a brain? Seriously, brains don’t come with operating manuals. I hope the book reaches readers who are curious about animals, their own mental well-being, or how brains work. Because brains change throughout life—“from the womb to the tomb,” as I often say—these questions concern all of us.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are your major messages?

KL: I begin by asking how rats, and later mice, came to dominate so much biomedical research. It’s a fascinating history involving rat-baiting competitions, a royal rat catcher in nineteenth-century London, raccoons that escaped early research settings, and the practical difficulty of capturing and maintaining wild animals.

From there, I explore intelligence, parenting, stress and coping, aging, and some wonderfully unexpected animal behavior. The book draws on my research and work by many other scientists. Prairie voles have helped us investigate social bonds; naked mole-rats raise intriguing questions about aging and disease; and research on animal hormones, including work with Gila monsters and their appetite-suppressing peptide, contributed to the development of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs. These examples show the benefits of paying attention to the distinctive biology and lives of other species.

One central message in Wild Brains is that context matters. Laboratory studies have taught us a great deal, but an animal’s housing, opportunities, and daily experiences influence the brain and behavior we observe. I propose more “living laboratories” that bring elements of natural habitats into research settings, alongside carefully designed ways to study animals in the wild. I also imagine more ambitious semi-natural settings—what I call biodomes—that reflect aspects of a species’ terrain, climate, and social world.

Scientists make influential decisions about the worlds our research animals inhabit. We can acknowledge that those decisions influence our research, and carefully consider habitats that support optimal behavioral responses in research models.

MB: How does your work differ from that of others concerned with similar topics?

KL: I have a foot in both the laboratory and the field, and I appreciate what each can reveal. Controlled experiments let us investigate mechanisms that would be difficult to isolate in nature. Field research lets scientists investigate behavioral scenarios we might never think to recreate in a lab.

New tools for tracking and observing animals make it increasingly possible to ask meaningful questions about free-ranging animals while minimizing disturbance. In the lab, I’d like us to become more comfortable with complexity, including richer environments, more opportunities for animals to make choices, and greater attention to their natural behavior. Comparative neuroendocrinologist Frank Beach urged researchers decades ago to study a broader range of animals and behaviors, all while embracing the messiness of “real life” in the laboratory. His challenge still feels timely.

MB: Are you hopeful that learning more about animal brains in the wild will also help us understand ourselves?

KL: Very much so. Comparing wild rats with laboratory rats has already revealed striking differences in their brains and physiology, including brain size, aspects of neural and vascular structure, and stress hormone levels. Those findings raise questions we could not ask if we assumed the laboratory rat represented the full range of rat responses.

I’m cautious about translating any finding directly from a rat—or any other animal—to a human. But a wider view of animal lives can help us ask better questions about how experience shapes resilience, learning, and mental health. I hope Wild Brains sparks curiosity in readers and makes room for research that takes the complexity of animals’ lives seriously.

item.title: Depression as a Functional Signal
item.description:
Depression

Depression as a Functional Signal

What depression may be asking us to change.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • The chemical imbalance theory of depression has no solid evidence behind it.
  • An evolutionary view sees depression as a signal that something in life isn't working.
  • Depression may push us to change by first making us withdraw from a life that no longer fits.

Some of the common characteristics of depression are:

  • Low motivation
  • Anhedonia (the loss of pleasure)
  • Pessimism about the future
  • Rumination about what might have gone wrong

These features of depression are exactly what make it so paralyzing: they make it difficult to continue with life as usual.

Source: Antoni Shkraba / Pexels

For decades, the standard explanation has been that something has gone wrong in the brain—that depression stems from a chemical imbalance that can be corrected with drugs.

But the chemical imbalance theory has little to support it. Despite decades of research, nobody has found solid evidence that depressed people have lower serotonin than anyone else—or any other known brain dysfunction.

There is a powerful alternative, one that dispenses entirely with the broken-brain metaphor. And it offers a surprising answer to why depression is so paralyzing.

Depression as Adaptation

In 2000, the psychiatrist and evolutionary biologist Randolph Nesse published a paper titled "Is Depression an Adaptation?" Since then, it's been the subject of numerous scholarly papers (see here for a recent review).

Just as there are physical adaptations, like hands for grasping, there are psychological ones. The purpose of rage is to enforce boundaries. The purpose of sexual desire is procreation. The purpose of pain is to alert us that something is wrong with our body.

You might think depression happens when one of these psychological adaptations breaks down—a defect or dysfunction in our normal capacity for sadness. But Nesse proposed something radical: that low mood—and perhaps some depression—isn't a breakdown at all, but a response shaped by natural selection to help us cope when our efforts in life aren't working.

If so, it has a purpose, or function, and sometimes we stay sick because we don't know what its purpose is.

What's the Purpose of Depression?

If depression has a purpose, what is it? At the most general level, we can say that depression is your brain's functional signal that something in your life is not going well and needs more attention. Its purpose is to disrupt a life path that isn't suited to you, such as a job, a relationship, or a long-term goal.

Consider a middle-aged woman: a successful entrepreneur with a happy family. Suppose she suddenly sinks into a deep depression—"out of the blue," as we like to say. Everything looks fine from the outside, but she's paralyzed by hopelessness and futility. Surely this is a brain defect?

Not necessarily. Her depression may be a signal. It's a message from the depths of her mind, just like pain. It's a message that there's some aspect of her life that she's deeply unsatisfied with, but that she's managed to set aside until now.

Why Is It So Paralyzing?

This brings us back to the puzzle. If depression is there to help you make positive life changes, why are depressed people so often incapable of making those changes? Why would a signal designed to help us change take away the energy we need to start a new career or relationship, or to pursue a new life goal?

The reason depression is so paralyzing is that it leads us to change by making us withdraw from a situation that no longer suits us. By sapping motivation and pleasure, it disrupts our ability to continue with business as usual. It's the brain's way of saying "I quit." It's a quiet form of rebellion.

In the best of cases, this period of depression is meant to lead us to insights about how we can grow, and about what a better life would look like.

What Does This Mean for Us?

This paradigm gives us a powerful tool for working through depression: Instead of fighting it off as the enemy, we want to listen to what it's trying to say.

The first question this paradigm prompts us to ask is: What aspect of my life is it pointing to? What needs to change? The answer might be obvious—but it might not be. In that case, it might help to find a therapist who's open to this paradigm.

A good therapist can not only help you figure out the source of your depression but also help you come up with a reasonable action plan that you can carry out without uprooting your whole life.

For example, the woman I described earlier doesn't necessarily need to leave her husband, quit her business, and move out to the woods.

The solution might be more modest: to hire an assistant to help with the business; to arrange to spend one weekend a month pursuing a creative endeavor she's left behind; to work with her family to come up with a better household division of labor.

Is All Depression Functional?

The evolutionary theorists don't think every single instance of depression has a function or purpose. They recognize that in some cases depression might stem from a brain dysfunction.

But current evidence suggests that about 80 percent of depression cases are attributable to a life event.

Sometimes, then, we won't know whether a person's depression is functional or dysfunctional. The solution isn't to abandon the function paradigm but to think of it as a first-line intervention for otherwise healthy adults.

If changes aren't happening within a few months, that may be a good time to consider other options, like antidepressants. This simply follows a basic principle of medicine: Try the least invasive treatment first.

My focus here is on mild to moderate depression. Severe depression can lead to suicidal ideation or even suicide attempts. In those cases, the first priority is getting the person to safety, then working out the best approach in coordination with a doctor.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Pesticides Threaten Farmers' Mental Health
item.description:
Health

Pesticides Threaten Farmers' Mental Health

Pesticide exposure may increase depression and disrupt brain and gut health.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Pesticides may disrupt the gut-brain connection and harm neurological health.
  • Pesticide exposure is linked to higher rates of depression among farmers.
  • Exposure can affect fetal brain development and increase risks during early life.
  • Economic hardship and weak protections can intensify pesticide exposure risks.
Source: Chris Ensminger / Unsplash

By Adrian Parham and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

During the 20th century, the Green Revolution transformed agriculture, ushering in new technologies that dramatically boosted food production. Among these advancements, pesticides became a staple in modern farming. While they helped create a surplus of food, there are concerns that pesticides have corroded the environment, contaminating the food supply and harming the neurological health of the very farmers who rely on them.

A recent article revealed a troubling link between pesticide exposure and depression among Brazilian farmers. Those who worked primarily with glyphosate reported significantly higher rates of depressive symptoms compared to those with less exposure. This study adds to the growing body of evidence linking pesticide use to a range of health issues, including Parkinson’s disease, birth defects, Alzheimer’s, congenital malformation, cancer, and depression.

A team of researchers examined the gut-brain connection in relation to pesticide exposure and proposed that the correlation between pesticide use and mental health disorders could be explained by the disruption of gut health. Conditions like irritable bowel syndrome, for instance, are often associated with higher levels of depression and anxiety, demonstrating the bidirectional communication between the digestive system and the brain.

The relationship is mediated by the enteric nervous system (ENS), often referred to as "the second brain," which regulates the gastrointestinal tract and relays information to the brain through the vagus nerve. While essential for maintaining both psychological and physiological well-being, this system is vulnerable. Many pesticides are capable of invading and disrupting this equilibrium.

Even more concerning is the impact on maternal gut health. Chemicals like glyphosate are known to cross the placenta, potentially dysregulating fetal brain development, an effect that may help explain the observed correlation between maternal pesticide exposure and birth defects. Pesticides can also infiltrate the developing brain through breast milk, compounding early-life exposure during critical stages of growth.

Tristan Bekinschtein, a researcher specializing in neuroscience and neurophysiology, prefaced that children are not the only ones with such vulnerability to pesticide exposure. Adults with chronic exposure have also reported motor dysfunction, mood disorders, and depressive symptoms.

Bekinschtein explains how exposure to pesticides not only harms the processes involved in the development of the brain, such as neurogenesis, but may also disrupt hormone balance, leading to irregularities in brain functioning. Additionally, prolonged exposure can trigger neuroinflammation and chronic stress, contributing to brain degeneration and hindering the brain’s ability to regulate itself.

While many of these observations were found in workers directly exposed to pesticides, nearby residents are not exempt from risk. In rural Chilean communities, individuals living close to pesticide-treated farms reported higher levels of depressive symptoms. Exposure often occurs through the inhalation of airborne chemicals carried by wind during spraying, as well as through contamination of soil and water.

Consumers also face potential dangers. A twin study found that those who consume conventionally grown vegetables, often sold in grocery stores, have higher levels of pesticide exposure. Despite growing public concerns, pesticide use is still on the rise. In 2024 alone, Canadians purchased 130 million kilograms of pesticides. Glyphosate usage has surged by 47 percent over the past decade. In fact, an estimated 70 percent of Canadians have detectable levels of glyphosate in their system.

Source: Jan Kopřiva / Unsplash

The long-term effects of exposure through contaminated food remain under investigation, but ongoing research is increasingly challenged by industry lobbying, with many millions being spent on lobbying efforts by pesticide manufacturers in the U.S. and around the world.

Alongside the neurological factors, Bekinschtein notes that social factors like education seem to also amplify the risks of pesticide exposure. Workers with lower levels of education tend to be more susceptible to harm, likely due to limited awareness about the dangers they face.

Even when they are aware, economic hardship and a lack of alternatives force them to continue working under dangerous conditions. Inadequate access to protective gear and safety measures further increases exposure. These risks are often compounded by broader economic and political conditions, which limit resources and enforcement in affected communities.

Some of the largest buyers of harmful pesticides are developing countries such as Costa Rica, Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Brazil. These nations often lack regulations, policies, and enforcement that protect workers and citizens. They are also especially vulnerable to lobbying.

In 2024, Mexico attempted to ban glyphosate and genetically modified corn due to concerns about safety, but relentless pressure by industry and the U.S. government delayed the ban, buying more time for pesticide manufacturers to tighten their grip on global agriculture.

Permitting corporate interests to endanger the health of farmers is not only a policy failure; it is a profound ethical one. Compromising the mental and physical health of farmers keeps these groups marginalized and challenges their ability to live healthy lives.

Adrian Parham is a research student at York University.
